extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science communicators, press officers, and journalists interested in health/science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and measuring instances where academic press releases or news stories make claims beyond the associated peer‑reviewed research (e.g., unwarranted advice, causal claims from correlational data, or over‑generalizing animal results to humans). Uses retrospective quantitative content analysis to compare press releases, journal articles, and news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to readers to change behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to readers to change behaviour that went beyond those in the associated peer reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as instances where press releases or news stories contained recommendations for readers to change behaviour that were not present in the peer‑reviewed article. In this study 40% of press releases contained such exaggerated advice; when present in press releases, 58% (95% CI 48% to 68%) of related news stories contained similar exaggeration versus 17% (10% to 24%) when press releases were not exaggerated. Odds ratio for this category: 6.5 (95% CI 3.5 to 12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal statements drawn from correlational research
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal statements drawn from correlational research that go beyond what is supported by the peer reviewed paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts as exaggeration when press releases or news articles imply causation from studies that are correlational. In the sample, 33% of press releases contained exaggerated causal claims; when press releases were exaggerated, 81% (95% CI 70% to 93%) of news stories contained similar exaggeration versus 18% (9% to 27%) when not. Odds ratio: 20 (95% CI 7.6 to 51).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference to humans from animal research beyond the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference to humans from animal research that extends beyond the inferences made in the associated peer reviewed paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deemed exaggeration when press releases or news translate animal findings into human implications not warranted by the original paper. In this study 36% of press releases contained such exaggerated inference; 86% (95% CI 77% to 95%) of news stories showed similar exaggeration when the press release did, versus 10% (0% to 19%) when it did not. Odds ratio: 56 (95% CI 15 to 211).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of exaggeration (discrepancy with peer‑reviewed paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is defined as press releases or news containing advice, causal claims, or human inferences from animal work that go beyond those in the associated peer‑reviewed papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured via retrospective quantitative content analysis comparing each press release and its associated peer‑reviewed paper and news stories. Sample: 462 press releases from 20 leading UK universities (2011), associated papers and 668 news stories. Outcomes reported as proportions with 95% CIs, odds ratios, and bootstrapped CIs; simulations accompany the analysis. This definition is the basis for coding and comparing materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake (presence and volume of news coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a press release had any news uptake (at least one related news story) and the mean number of news stories per press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess whether exaggeration in press releases increases media coverage. The study found the proportion of press releases with some news uptake and the mean number of news stories per press release were not statistically distinguishable between exaggerated and non‑exaggerated press releases (bootstrapped 95% CIs reported).
